extracted.intended_audience: educated lay readers and general natural philosophers interested in natural theology (readers not expert in advanced mathematics)
extracted.subtask_description: Constructing/explaining an empirical, quantitative argument (natural-philosophical and theological) that uses microscope observations, order-of-magnitude estimates, and accessible mathematics to argue for divine providence. The piece is aimed at non-specialist readers and emphasizes intelligibility and conservative assumptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inverse-square law for light
rubrics_metrics.description: “the Number of the Particles of Light in two equally great, but unequally distant, Places from the Flame, are to each other in an inverted Ratio of the Squares of their Distances.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the inverse-square relation to compute how particle counts change with distance from a point source; this principle underpins later counts (see Num. X and references to Contemplation XXIV).

rubrics_metrics.name: Partition the ray into observable units (animalcula-lengths)
rubrics_metrics.description: “we have only adapted our Divisions to such Parts as are equal to the Space fill'd by each of those Animalcula that are visible thro' a Microscope”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When discretizing a spatial extent for counting particles, divide it into segments equal to the smallest empirically observable units (animalcula seen under the microscope) rather than invoking abstract infinitesimal parts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Represent particle counts by perpendiculars and sum them
rubrics_metrics.description: “Let there be perpendicular Lines of an indefinite Length drawn upon the Points A, B, C, D, and all the Partitions of these Lengths of the Animalcula … in order to describe thereby the Number of Light-Particles which are to be found in the Space of each particular Animalculum.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Map each partition to a perpendicular whose length equals the particle-count for that partition; the total number in the ray is the sum of these perpendiculars (geometric/graphical bookkeeping).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use conservative (smaller) estimates to avoid overclaiming
rubrics_metrics.description: “That we may not therefore be deceiv'd in our Calculation, we shall make choice of a much smaller Sum than we need do, and therefore only retain the Number 10<2, that alone being the greatest Quantity … and we will throw away the rest Bb, Cc, Dd, &c.” (Num. XVII)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer underestimates (dropping many positive contributions) so conclusions remain compelling even under cautious assumptions; explicitly state when larger discarded terms would only strengthen the result.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer intelligibility over advanced mathematic methods for lay readers
rubrics_metrics.description: “What we here write is not so much for great Mathematicians, as for others that are of a good natural Understanding, tho' not thoroughly vers'd in Lines and Figures; wherefore, when we can use other Methods of Proving, we avoid much as possible those of the Mathematicians … my chief End being to render myself intelligible even to the meanest Capacity.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When addressing non-specialist audiences, avoid heavy formal mathematical techniques (e.g., Wallis' methods, infinite calculus) in favor of simpler, more transparent demonstrations and prose.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anchor numerical estimates to empirical measures and contemporary authorities
rubrics_metrics.description: Examples: adopting Leuwenhoek's counts of animalcula per inch/foot, Boyle's experiments on copper dissolution, and French astronomers' measure of Earth's diameter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Base large-number estimates on published empirical observations and respected authorities; state the adopted empirical assumptions (e.g., '1,000,000,000 of those Animalcula make up one Grain of Sand', '100 Sands equal one Inch').

rubrics_metrics.name: Use unit-consistent dimensional reasoning
rubrics_metrics.description: The text repeatedly converts between diameters, inches, feet and grains (e.g., '10 Diameters of the Animalcula make the Length of one Foot, and 10== of the same, the Length of OE, or 10,000 Feet').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep clear and consistent unit definitions when scaling microscopic counts to macroscopic volumes (explicitly state how many observable units equal an inch/foot/grain).

rubrics_metrics.name: Demonstrative experiments as rhetorical proof (smoke/benjoin and dissolution)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use small, repeatable experiments—e.g., diffusing a small quantity of benjoin in a room to estimate particles per cubic inch, Boyle dissolving copper to tint many grains of water—to show the fineness and determinacy of particles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide simple experimental set-ups and computations (room volume → cubic inches → visible particle size) to make the magnitude arguments concrete and persuasive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relate quantitative natural observations to theological claims
rubrics_metrics.description: The author explicitly connects the smallness/number of particles to arguments for divine providence and scriptural passages (e.g., hairs of the head numbered: 'Math. x. 30').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When the rhetorical aim is theological persuasion, tie empirical magnitudes and regularities to scriptural or doctrinal claims to strengthen the moral/philosophical conclusion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Order-of-magnitude arithmetic and rounding for tractability
rubrics_metrics.description: Multiple instances of rounding/choosing convenient digits to prevent disputes: 'Now in Ses. XVI, the Number there found was 44 Figures ... let us for Conveniency ... suppose that both the first Figures were a (1,) and the rest Cyphers or Noughts.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Clearly state rounding conventions and simplifications used in very large-number calculations, and note how such choices affect (or do not overturn) the qualitative conclusion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explain and justify methodological omissions to readers
rubrics_metrics.description: The author pre-empts objections: he explains why he omitted approximation/infinite-division methods (they presuppose infinite small parts) and why he chose simpler empirical partitions instead.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When skipping standard formal methods, state the reason (accessibility, empirical grounding) so readers understand the limitations and appropriateness of the approach.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use multiple independent lines of evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: The argument draws on geometric/inverse-square reasoning, microscope observations, combustion/flux of light estimates, dissolution/tinting experiments, and atmospheric/meteorological phenomena to converge on the same conclusion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Support a broad conclusion by combining independent empirical and theoretical arguments rather than relying on a single calculation or experiment.
